groups.title: MongoDB document model and schema design
groups.question: You are designing MongoDB documents for tasks, their comments and the users assigned to them. Explain how you would structure the data and what MongoDB stores beyond plain JSON.

followUps.Embedding versus referencing: choosing t: When would you embed comments inside a task and when reference users by id?
followUps.BSON types: ObjectId, Date, and Int64 be: What types does BSON add, and what is special about ObjectId?

evidence.text: Embed data that is always read with its parent and stays small, like a task's comments.
Reference data that is large, shared or updated on its own, like users.
Embedding data that grows without limit can hit document size limits and slow writes.
BSON adds types JSON lacks, such as ObjectId, dates and specific integer sizes.
An ObjectId includes a timestamp, so ids roughly sort by creation time.
Storing dates as real date types allows correct sorting and range queries.

notEnough: Only saying BSON is binary JSON.

groups.title: Mongoose schema validation and middleware hooks
groups.question: Tasks are saved with missing titles, and user passwords must always be hashed before saving no matter which code saves them. Explain how Mongoose schemas and hooks handle this.

followUps.Schema types, validators, required, and: What do required, default and validators in a Mongoose schema do?
followUps.Pre/post hooks for cross-cutting concern: How would a pre-save hook hash passwords, and why check isModified?

evidence.text: The schema defines each field's type, whether it is required and its default.
Mongoose validates documents before saving them.
This adds application-level rules on top of MongoDB, which accepts any document by default.
A pre-save hook runs before a document is saved.
It can hash the password automatically so no code path forgets.
Checking that the password was modified avoids hashing an already-hashed value again.

notEnough: Only saying hooks run before save.

groups.title: CRUD and querying with Mongoose
groups.question: You are writing endpoints that list open tasks due today, update a task and return the updated version. Explain the Mongoose methods and query operators you would use.

followUps.Model.find(), findById(), create(), find: Why pass new and runValidators to findByIdAndUpdate?
followUps.Query operators: $in, $gte, $regex, and: How would you find tasks with several allowed statuses that are due before a date?

evidence.text: find, findById, create and findByIdAndUpdate cover most create, read and update work.
new returns the updated document instead of the old one.
runValidators applies schema validation on updates, which is off by default.
$in matches any value from a list, such as several statuses.
Comparison operators like $lte filter by ranges such as due dates.
$or combines alternative conditions and $regex matches text patterns.

groups.title: Connections, indexes, and population
groups.question: Your API connects to MongoDB on every request, slows down as tasks grow, and returns assignee ids instead of names. Explain how you would manage connections, indexes and related data.

followUps.mongoose.connect with connection event h: How should a Node app connect to MongoDB?
followUps.Mongoose populate for resolving ObjectId: What does populate do, and what does it cost?

evidence.text: Connect once at startup and reuse the connection pool.
Listen for connection and error events to log and react to problems.
Set sensible timeouts so a missing database fails clearly instead of hanging.
populate replaces stored ids with fields from the referenced documents.
You can choose which fields to bring in, like name and email.
It runs extra queries behind the scenes, so populating large lists can be slow.
